subject: Biology
text: Living organisms show defining features: metabolism (sum of all chemical reactions), growth (increase in mass/number — internal in living beings), reproduction, cellular organisation, consciousness/response to stimuli, and self-replication. Metabolism and cellular organisation are the most defining. Taxonomy is classification and naming of organisms; systematics studies diversity and relationships. Taxonomic hierarchy (descending): Kingdom, Phylum/Division, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. Species is the basic unit. Binomial nomenclature (Carolus Linnaeus): each organism has a two-word Latin name — genus (capitalised) + species (small), italicised or underlined, e.g. Mangifera indica. Taxonomic aids: herbarium, botanical gardens, museum, zoological parks, keys, flora, manuals, monographs, catalogues.

subject: Biology
text: Whittaker's five-kingdom classification (1969): Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia — based on cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition and reproduction. Monera: prokaryotes (bacteria, cyanobacteria); autotrophic or heterotrophic; includes archaebacteria (extreme habitats) and eubacteria. Protista: single-celled eukaryotes (Chrysophytes, Dinoflagellates, Euglenoids, Slime moulds, Protozoans). Fungi: heterotrophic, saprophytic/parasitic, cell wall of chitin (Phycomycetes, Ascomycetes, Basidiomycetes, Deuteromycetes); many form symbiotic lichens (with algae) and mycorrhiza (with plant roots). Plantae: multicellular autotrophs with cellulose cell walls. Animalia: multicellular heterotrophs, no cell wall. Viruses, viroids, prions and lichens are not placed in these kingdoms; viruses are non-cellular (nucleic acid + protein coat).

subject: Biology
text: Plant kingdom classification: Algae, Bryophytes, Pteridophytes, Gymnosperms, Angiosperms. Algae: simple, autotrophic, aquatic (Chlorophyceae-green, Phaeophyceae-brown, Rhodophyceae-red). Bryophytes ('amphibians of the plant kingdom', e.g. moss, Marchantia): need water for fertilisation, dominant gametophyte. Pteridophytes (ferns): first true vascular plants (xylem, phloem), dominant sporophyte. Gymnosperms: naked seeds (not enclosed in fruit), e.g. Pinus, Cycas. Angiosperms (flowering plants): seeds enclosed in fruit; divided into monocots (one cotyledon) and dicots (two cotyledons). Alternation of generations: life cycle alternates between haploid gametophyte and diploid sporophyte. Trend across groups: gametophyte reduces and sporophyte becomes dominant and independent.

subject: Biology
text: Animals classified by body organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation, and notochord. Basis: levels of organisation (cellular, tissue, organ, organ-system); symmetry (asymmetrical, radial, bilateral); diploblastic (2 germ layers) or triploblastic (3); coelom (acoelomate, pseudocoelomate, coelomate). Major phyla: Porifera (sponges), Coelenterata/Cnidaria (Hydra, jellyfish — diploblastic, radial), Platyhelminthes (flatworms), Aschelminthes (roundworms), Annelida (earthworm — true coelom, segmented), Arthropoda (largest phylum — insects, jointed legs), Mollusca (snail, octopus), Echinodermata (starfish — spiny, radial adults), Chordata (notochord). Chordata subphylum Vertebrata includes classes: Cyclostomata, Chondrichthyes (cartilage fish), Osteichthyes (bony fish), Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves (birds), Mammalia. Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, and pharyngeal gill slits are chordate features.

subject: Biology
text: Root system: tap root (dicots) and fibrous/adventitious (monocots); regions — root cap, meristematic, elongation, maturation; modifications for storage (carrot), support (prop roots) and respiration. Stem: bears nodes, internodes, buds; modifications (tendrils, thorns, tubers-potato, rhizome). Leaf: flat photosynthetic organ; parts — base, petiole, lamina; venation reticulate (dicot) or parallel (monocot); simple vs compound; phyllotaxy (arrangement). Inflorescence: racemose (main axis grows) or cymose (terminal flower). Flower: reproductive unit — calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens), gynoecium (carpels); aestivation, placentation. Fruit: develops from ovary; true and false fruits. Seed: dicot (two cotyledons) and monocot (one). Floral formula and diagram summarise flower structure. Example families: Fabaceae, Solanaceae, Liliaceae.

subject: Biology
text: Plant tissues: meristematic (dividing — apical, intercalary, lateral) and permanent (simple: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma; complex: xylem for water conduction, phloem for food conduction). Tissue systems: epidermal (protection, with stomata), ground, and vascular. Xylem: tracheids, vessels, fibre, parenchyma; conducts water upward. Phloem: sieve tubes, companion cells, fibre, parenchyma; conducts food. Monocot vs dicot anatomy: dicot stem has vascular bundles in a ring (open, with cambium); monocot has scattered bundles (closed, no cambium). Roots: dicot has few xylem bundles, monocot has many (polyarch). Secondary growth: increase in girth due to vascular cambium and cork cambium, forming annual rings, wood (secondary xylem) and bark.

subject: Biology
text: Animal tissues are of four types: (1) Epithelial — covering/lining (squamous, cuboidal, columnar; glandular); cells tightly packed on a basement membrane. (2) Connective — most abundant; links and supports (loose/areolar, dense, specialised: cartilage, bone, blood, adipose); has abundant matrix. (3) Muscular — contractile (skeletal/striated-voluntary, smooth-involuntary, cardiac-heart). (4) Nervous — neurons and neuroglia; conducts impulses. Organ: made of tissues; organ system: group of organs performing a function. Example study organism — the cockroach (Periplaneta): body divided into head, thorax, abdomen; open circulatory system, malpighian tubules for excretion. Frog is a common vertebrate example studied for morphology and organ systems (poikilothermic amphibian).

subject: Biology
text: Cell theory (Schleiden, Schwann; Virchow added 'omnis cellula-e cellula' — all cells arise from pre-existing cells): all living organisms are made of cells, the basic structural and functional unit of life. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria): no true nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; have nucleoid, 70S ribosomes, cell wall, sometimes capsule, flagella, plasmids, mesosomes. Eukaryotic cells: true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Cell membrane (fluid mosaic model, Singer and Nicolson) is selectively permeable. Organelles: nucleus (DNA, nucleolus), endoplasmic reticulum (rough with ribosomes-protein synthesis; smooth-lipid), Golgi apparatus (packaging/secretion), mitochondria (powerhouse-ATP), plastids/chloroplast (photosynthesis, in plants), lysosomes (digestion), ribosomes (protein synthesis), vacuole. Plant cells have a cell wall (cellulose), large vacuole and plastids; animal cells have centrioles.

subject: Biology
text: Biomolecules are chemical compounds in living cells. Carbohydrates: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose), disaccharides (sucrose), polysaccharides (starch, cellulose, glycogen). Proteins: polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; structure — primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary; functions include enzymes, transport, structure. Lipids: fats, oils, phospholipids; energy storage and membranes. Nucleic acids (DNA, RNA): polymers of nucleotides (nitrogen base + sugar + phosphate); store and express genetic information. Enzymes are biological catalysts (mostly proteins) that lower activation energy; properties — specificity, affected by temperature and pH; active site binds substrate. Enzyme action: 'lock and key' / induced fit. Cofactors (coenzymes, metal ions) assist enzymes. Metabolites: primary (essential — amino acids, sugars) and secondary (alkaloids, pigments).

subject: Biology
text: The cell cycle has interphase (G1 growth, S — DNA replication, G2 growth) and the M phase (division). Mitosis: division of somatic cells producing two identical diploid daughter cells; stages — prophase (chromosomes condense, spindle forms), metaphase (chromosomes at equator), anaphase (sister chromatids separate to poles), telophase (nuclei reform); followed by cytokinesis. Mitosis is used for growth, repair and cell replacement. Meiosis: reductional division in reproductive cells producing four haploid cells; two divisions (Meiosis I and II). Meiosis I is reductional (homologous chromosomes separate; crossing over in prophase I gives genetic variation); Meiosis II is like mitosis. Significance of meiosis: maintains constant chromosome number across generations and creates variation. Significance of mitosis: growth and maintenance.

subject: Biology
text: Photosynthesis: green plants make food using light. Overall: 6CO2 + 12H2O -> (light, chlorophyll) C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O. Site: chloroplast — grana (thylakoids) and stroma. Two phases: (1) Light reaction (in thylakoid membranes): chlorophyll absorbs light, water splits (photolysis) releasing O2, produces ATP (photophosphorylation) and NADPH. Photosystems PS I and PS II; electron transport (Z-scheme). (2) Dark reaction/Calvin cycle (in stroma): CO2 fixed using ATP and NADPH to form sugar; the enzyme RuBisCO fixes CO2. C3 plants (Calvin cycle, first product 3-carbon PGA); C4 plants (Hatch-Slack pathway, Kranz anatomy, efficient in hot climates, first product 4-carbon OAA). Photorespiration occurs in C3 plants (wasteful). Factors: light, CO2, temperature, water (law of limiting factors — Blackman).

subject: Biology
text: Cellular respiration breaks down glucose to release energy (ATP). Glycolysis (in cytoplasm, common to all): glucose (6C) -> 2 pyruvate (3C) + 2 ATP + 2 NADH. Aerobic respiration (needs O2, in mitochondria): pyruvate enters the Krebs cycle (citric acid/TCA cycle) producing CO2, NADH, FADH2, and ATP; then the electron transport chain (ETC, oxidative phosphorylation) on the inner mitochondrial membrane produces most ATP, with O2 as the final electron acceptor forming water. Total ~36-38 ATP per glucose (aerobic). Anaerobic respiration/fermentation (no O2): in yeast glucose -> ethanol + CO2; in muscle/some cells -> lactic acid; yields only 2 ATP. Respiratory Quotient (RQ) = volume of CO2 released / volume of O2 consumed (1 for carbohydrates). Amphibolic pathway: respiration involves both breakdown (catabolism) and building (anabolism).

subject: Biology
text: Growth is an irreversible increase in size/mass; development includes growth and differentiation. Phases of growth: meristematic, elongation, maturation. Growth is measurable (arithmetic and geometric); growth rate shows a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve. Differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation shape plant cells. Plant growth regulators (phytohormones): (1) Auxins — cell elongation, apical dominance, rooting; (2) Gibberellins (GA) — stem elongation, seed germination, bolting; (3) Cytokinins — cell division, delay senescence; (4) Ethylene — fruit ripening, ageing, abscission (a gaseous hormone); (5) Abscisic acid (ABA) — 'stress hormone', closes stomata, inhibits growth, dormancy. Photoperiodism: flowering response to day/night length (short-day, long-day, day-neutral plants). Vernalisation: promotion of flowering by low temperature.

subject: Biology
text: Human respiratory system: nostrils -> nasal cavity -> pharynx -> larynx -> trachea -> bronchi -> bronchioles -> alveoli (site of gas exchange). Breathing (pulmonary ventilation): inspiration (diaphragm and external intercostals contract, thoracic volume increases, air enters) and expiration (muscles relax, air pushed out). Respiratory volumes: tidal volume (TV ~500 mL), inspiratory/expiratory reserve, residual volume, vital capacity. Gas exchange: O2 diffuses from alveoli into blood, CO2 from blood into alveoli (by pressure gradients). Transport of O2: mostly by haemoglobin (oxyhaemoglobin); CO2 transported as bicarbonate, carbamino-haemoglobin, and dissolved. Oxygen dissociation curve is sigmoid. Breathing is regulated by the respiratory centre in the medulla. Disorders: asthma, emphysema, occupational respiratory disorders.

subject: Biology
text: Blood is a fluid connective tissue: plasma (55%, water + proteins like albumin/globulin/fibrinogen) and formed elements (RBCs/erythrocytes with haemoglobin, WBCs/leucocytes for immunity, platelets for clotting). Blood groups: ABO system (A, B, AB, O) and Rh factor; important for transfusion. Lymph is tissue fluid that returns to blood and aids immunity. Human heart (in the thoracic cavity): four chambers — two atria and two ventricles; valves (tricuspid, bicuspid/mitral, semilunar) prevent backflow. Double circulation: pulmonary (heart-lungs) and systemic (heart-body). The heartbeat is myogenic, initiated by the SA node (pacemaker); cardiac cycle (systole/diastole). ECG records electrical activity. Blood pressure normal ~120/80 mmHg. Disorders: hypertension, coronary artery disease, angina, heart failure.

subject: Biology
text: Excretion removes nitrogenous wastes. Based on the waste, animals are ammonotelic (ammonia, aquatic), ureotelic (urea, mammals), or uricotelic (uric acid, birds/reptiles). Human excretory system: two kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, urethra. The nephron is the functional unit (~1 million per kidney): glomerulus + Bowman's capsule (filtration), proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule, collecting duct. Urine formation: (1) glomerular filtration (blood filtered under pressure), (2) tubular reabsorption (glucose, water, ions reabsorbed), (3) tubular secretion (H+, K+, ammonia secreted). Counter-current mechanism (loop of Henle + vasa recta) concentrates urine. Regulation: hormones ADH (water reabsorption), aldosterone, and RAAS. Other excretory organs: lungs (CO2), skin (sweat), liver (bile). Disorders: uremia, dialysis for kidney failure.

subject: Biology
text: Movement is a characteristic of living beings; locomotion is movement causing change of place. Types of movement: amoeboid (pseudopodia), ciliary (cilia/flagella), and muscular (by muscles + skeleton). Muscle types: skeletal (striated, voluntary), smooth (visceral, involuntary), cardiac (heart). Skeletal muscle structure: muscle -> fascicle -> muscle fibre -> myofibril -> sarcomere (functional unit) with actin (thin) and myosin (thick) filaments. Muscle contraction: sliding filament theory — actin slides over myosin, using ATP and Ca2+, triggered by a nerve impulse. Skeletal system: axial (skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum) and appendicular (limbs, girdles); total 206 bones in adults. Joints: fibrous (immovable), cartilaginous, synovial (freely movable — ball-and-socket, hinge). Disorders: arthritis, osteoporosis, gout, muscular dystrophy, myasthenia gravis.

subject: Biology
text: The nervous system provides rapid coordination. Neuron (functional unit): dendrites (receive), cell body, axon (transmit); myelinated/unmyelinated. Nerve impulse: resting potential (polarised, negative inside) -> action potential (depolarisation by Na+ influx) travels along the axon -> transmission across a synapse via neurotransmitters (chemical) or electrically. Human nervous system: Central Nervous System (brain + spinal cord) and Peripheral Nervous System (somatic + autonomic — sympathetic and parasympathetic). Brain parts: forebrain (cerebrum — thinking; thalamus; hypothalamus — controls hunger, temperature, hormones), midbrain, hindbrain (cerebellum — balance; pons; medulla — controls heartbeat, breathing). Reflex action and reflex arc give quick involuntary responses via the spinal cord. Sense organs: eye (photoreception — rods and cones) and ear (hearing and balance).

subject: Biology
text: The endocrine system provides slower, chemical coordination via hormones (secreted by ductless glands into blood). Major glands and hormones: Hypothalamus (releasing/inhibiting hormones, controls pituitary). Pituitary ('master gland'): GH (growth), TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin, ADH, oxytocin. Thyroid: thyroxine (T3, T4 — needs iodine; regulates metabolism; deficiency causes goitre/hypothyroidism). Parathyroid: PTH (calcium balance). Adrenal: adrenaline/noradrenaline ('fight or flight'), cortisol, aldosterone. Pancreas (islets of Langerhans): insulin (lowers blood glucose) and glucagon (raises it); insulin deficiency causes diabetes mellitus. Gonads: testis — testosterone; ovary — estrogen, progesterone. Pineal: melatonin (sleep-wake rhythm). Hormones act via receptors; feedback regulation maintains balance (homeostasis). Hormonal and neural systems work together to coordinate body functions.
